newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7, IN FAINT ECHO OF PAST, SEEK STABLE DOLLAR.
newsitem.headline: G7, IN FAINT ECHO OF PAST, SEEK STABLE DOLLAR.

text.p: An agreement struck this weekend by the Group of Seven industrial nations to try to stabilise the dollar faintly echoes the landmark Louvre accord they reached 10 years ago this month.
But it is not nearly as ambitious as that now-discredited pact, which unsuccessfully sought to hold currency rates in target zones intervention in the foreign exchange market.
"The Berlin message is not comparable to the ... Louvre accord," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said.

In a statement released after a meeting on Saturday, the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- signalled their desire for stability in the foreign exchange markets by saying that their currencies were no longer misaligned in a major way.
"We reaffirmed our view that exchange rates should reflect fundamentals and that excess volatility is undesirable," the Group added.

A stable dollar would help quiet U.S. exporters complaints that they are being put at a disadvantage on world markets. It would also help buttress the shaky Japanese stock market and dampen any potential inflationary threat in Germany.
The dollar closed in New York on Friday at just over 123 Japanese yen and 1.66 German marks. That is well above the lows set in 1995 of just under 80 yen and just over 1.34 marks.

Although the G7 statement left open the possibility that it might intervene in the currency markets at some point to stabilse the dollar, finance ministers from several nations said that no plan to do so was reached here.

"We reached no agreement of that kind today. We didn't think it was necessary," British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said, adding, "We don't have any set targets for the exchange rate of any currency."

But that will not stop currency traders and speculators from trying to see how much of a movement in the dollar the G7 will tolerate -- either up or down. Traders and speculators make money from currency volatility, not stability.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin gave some indication of how much of a fall in the dollar he might be willing to accept when he declared that the U.S. currency has been strong "for some time now."
That remark appears to roughly cover the period of the last six months, back to the last G7 meeting, in Washington in September. At that time, the dollar was trading at about 110 yen and 1.52 marks.

A drop in the dollar back to those levels would clearly be welcomed by Japan, which has made no secret of its concern that the weak yen could trigger a massive sell-off in the shaky Tokyo stock market, hurting its banks and its economy.

But European countries have made equally clear that they would not be happy with a retracement of the dollar's gains of the past six months -- despite suggestions by a senior U.S. official implying otherwise.
"We are satisfied with the dollar," Germany's Waigel said. "Six months ago, we noted an incorrect development with the dollar. We wanted a stronger dollar and that is what we have."
It is even more unclear how much more of a rise of the dollar the G7 would be willing to tolerate from current levels.

Japan again would be the most uneasy, and might even intervene to sell dollars if the greenback pushed much higher now. But the past has shown that such unilateral action tends to be fruitless without support from the rest of the G7.
And that support does not seem to be forthcoming. Although Washington has subtly shifted its rhetoric on the dollar, that does not mean it is trying to cap the dollar's advance.
Rather, the United States appears to have adopted a symmetric approach to its currency -- neither trying to push it up or down.

As Rubin has said more than once, currency rates ultimately reflect fundamentals. And as he made clear at a news conference here, the fundamentals in Japan do not look very good, with both the economy and the banking system shaky.
